chapters.title: The gospel and mankind’s rejection of God

parts.text: Paul greets Rome’s saints as an apostle of the gospel promised in Scripture concerning Jesus Christ, David’s descendant and the risen Son of God. He thanks God for their faith and longs to visit for mutual encouragement. Unashamed of the gospel, he declares it God’s power to save everyone believing, Jew and Greek, revealing righteousness received by faith.

God’s wrath is revealed against ungodliness. Creation makes his power and Godhead known, leaving people without excuse. Rejecting gratitude and exchanging God’s glory for idols darken their understanding. God gives them over to bodily dishonour, unnatural sexual relations, and a corrupt mind. Paul lists widespread evils and condemns both practicing them and approving others who do them despite knowing God’s judgment.

chapters.title: God judges impartially, beyond outward religious claims

parts.text: Those condemning others while doing the same things condemn themselves. God’s patience should lead to repentance, but hardened hearts store up wrath. He judges everyone according to deeds without favouritism toward Jew or Gentile. Possessing the law is insufficient without doing it. Even Gentiles without the law show its work in their hearts through conscience, and God will judge hidden things through Jesus Christ.

Paul challenges the Jew who boasts in knowing and teaching the law while breaking it. Such hypocrisy dishonours God and causes his name to be blasphemed among Gentiles. Circumcision does not excuse disobedience, nor does its absence negate obedience. True Jewish identity and circumcision are inward, of the heart and spirit, seeking God’s praise rather than human approval.

chapters.title: All have sinned; justification comes through faith

parts.text: Jews have the privilege of receiving God’s oracles, and human unbelief cannot cancel his faithfulness. Paul rejects arguments that wrongdoing becomes acceptable because it highlights God’s righteousness. Both Jews and Gentiles are under sin. Scriptural testimony exposes universal corruption in conduct and speech, leaving the world accountable. The law reveals sin rather than providing justification through its deeds.

God’s righteousness is now manifested apart from the law, though witnessed by the law and prophets. All have sinned, yet justification is freely given by grace through Christ’s redemption and faith in his blood. God remains just while justifying believers in Jesus. Boasting is excluded: one God justifies Jew and Gentile through faith, which establishes rather than nullifies the law.

chapters.title: Abraham’s faith was counted for righteousness

parts.text: Abraham’s example shows that righteousness is counted through believing God, not earned as wages. David likewise describes the blessedness of forgiven sin and righteousness imputed without works. Abraham received this righteousness before circumcision; circumcision became its sign and seal. He therefore stands as father of believing Gentiles and of circumcised people who follow his faith.

The promise rests on faith and grace rather than the law, making it sure to all Abraham’s believing seed. Against natural hope, he trusted God’s promise of descendants despite his aged body and Sara’s barrenness. Fully persuaded that God could perform his promise, he gave God glory. This record also concerns those believing in the God who raised Jesus, delivered for offences and raised for justification.

chapters.title: Peace through Christ and life beyond Adam’s offence

parts.text: Justification by faith brings peace with God, access to grace, and hope of glory through Jesus Christ. Even tribulations produce patience, experience, and hope, while the Holy Ghost assures believers of God’s love. Christ died for the ungodly and for sinners, demonstrating that love. Those reconciled through his death can trust his life to save them and rejoice in God.

Paul contrasts Adam and Christ. Through one man sin and death entered the world, and death spread to all. Christ’s free gift surpasses the offence, bringing justification and life where Adam’s disobedience brought condemnation. Those receiving grace and righteousness reign in life through Christ. The law makes offence abound, but grace abounds more, reigning through righteousness to eternal life.

chapters.title: Dead to sin and alive to God

parts.text: Grace does not justify continuing in sin. Those baptized into Christ share his death and burial so that, as he rose, they should walk in newness of life. Their old man is crucified with him, breaking sin’s service. They must reckon themselves dead to sin and alive to God, yielding their bodies as instruments of righteousness. Sin must not reign over those under grace.

Freedom from the law is no permission to sin: obedience reveals whom a person serves. The believers have obeyed the delivered teaching from the heart and become servants of righteousness. Their former service produced shame and death; service to God bears fruit in holiness and everlasting life. Sin pays death, but God gives eternal life through Jesus Christ.

chapters.title: The holy law exposes the struggle with sin

parts.text: Paul uses marriage to show that death ends the law’s binding claim. Through Christ’s body, believers have died to the law and belong to the risen Christ, bearing fruit for God in newness of spirit. The law itself is holy and good. Yet sin exploits its commandment, arousing forbidden desire, deceiving, and bringing death. The command exposes sin’s exceeding sinfulness.

Paul describes an inward conflict: he approves the good but does what he hates. Delight in God’s law meets another law in his members that brings captivity to sin. His desire to do right cannot by itself overcome the evil present. Crying out for deliverance from this body of death, he thanks God through Jesus Christ.

chapters.title: Life in the Spirit and unshakable love in Christ

parts.text: Those in Christ who walk after the Spirit are free from condemnation. God accomplishes through his Son what the law could not through weak flesh. A fleshly mind leads to death; the Spirit brings life, peace, and power to put sinful deeds to death. Those led by him receive adoption, cry to their Father, and become fellow heirs with Christ, sharing suffering and glory.

Present suffering cannot compare with coming glory. Creation groans for deliverance, and believers await their bodies’ redemption. The Spirit helps their prayers, and God works all things for good for those loving him and called according to his purpose. His purpose carries them toward Christ’s likeness and glory. With God justifying and Christ interceding, no suffering, power, or created thing can separate them from his love.

chapters.title: Israel’s privileges and God’s sovereign mercy

parts.text: Paul expresses deep sorrow for his fellow Israelites, who possess the covenants, law, worship, promises, and ancestry from which Christ came according to the flesh. God’s word has not failed: descent alone does not define the children of promise. Isaac’s birth and God’s choice concerning Jacob and Esau illustrate his purpose. Mercy rests on God who shows it, and Pharaoh illustrates his power to harden and display his name.

Paul answers objections by comparing God to a potter with authority over his vessels. Prophetic texts speak of Gentiles becoming God’s people and a remnant of Israel being saved. Gentiles attain righteousness through faith, while Israel stumbles by pursuing it through works rather than faith. The one who believes on God’s appointed stone will not be ashamed.

chapters.title: Israel’s need and the word of faith

parts.text: Paul prays for Israel’s salvation. Their zeal lacks knowledge because they seek their own righteousness instead of submitting to God’s. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to believers. The word of faith is near: confession of the Lord Jesus and heartfelt belief in his resurrection bring salvation. The same Lord is rich toward Jew and Greek, and whoever calls on his name will be saved.

Calling requires believing, believing requires hearing, and hearing requires a preacher who is sent. Yet not all obey the gospel. Faith comes by hearing God’s word. Paul uses Scripture to show that Israel has heard and has been warned of Gentiles finding God. God’s outstretched hands meet a disobedient and contradicting people.

chapters.title: A remnant, the olive tree, and promised mercy

parts.text: God has not cast away his people. Paul himself and the remnant chosen by grace demonstrate this, as did the faithful seven thousand in Elias’s day. Israel’s stumbling brings salvation to Gentiles and is intended to provoke Israel to jealousy. Gentile believers are compared to wild olive branches grafted among natural branches. They must not boast: they stand by faith and are warned that they too will be cut off if they do not continue in God’s goodness. Natural branches can be grafted in again if they do not remain in unbelief.

Paul reveals that Israel’s partial blindness lasts until the Gentiles’ fulness comes in, and declares that all Israel shall be saved through the promised Deliverer. Though enemies concerning the gospel, they remain beloved for the fathers’ sake; God’s gifts and calling do not change. Paul celebrates the depth of God’s wisdom and his mercy toward both groups.

chapters.title: A renewed life of service and sincere love

parts.text: Because of God’s mercies, believers should offer their bodies as living sacrifices and be transformed by renewed minds rather than conform to the world. Sober self-assessment replaces pride. As members of one body in Christ, they have different gifts and should exercise them faithfully, whether teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, leading, or showing mercy.

Love must be sincere, rejecting evil and holding to good. Paul urges brotherly affection, diligent service, hopeful patience, prayer, generosity, and hospitality. Believers should bless persecutors, share others’ joy and grief, and associate humbly. They must repay no evil, seek peace as far as possible, and leave vengeance to God. Feeding a hungry enemy exemplifies overcoming evil with good.

Paul calls for submission to governing authorities because authority is ordained by God. Rulers are described as God’s servants for good and as agents of punishment against wrongdoing. Submission should arise from conscience as well as fear of punishment. Believers must render taxes, duties, respect, and honour where these are due.

The continuing debt is love, which fulfils the law because it does no harm to a neighbour. Commandments against adultery, killing, stealing, false witness, and coveting are summed up in loving one’s neighbour as oneself. Knowing that salvation draws nearer, believers should awaken, cast off darkness, and put on light’s armour. They must live honestly, putting on Christ rather than providing for fleshly lusts.

chapters.title: Welcome one another without wounding conscience

parts.text: Believers should receive those weak in faith without quarrelling over disputed practices. Differences about food and observance of days must not produce contempt or condemnation. Each serves the Lord and should act with conviction and thanksgiving. Christ is Lord of the living and dead, and every person will give an account before his judgment seat.

Instead of judging a brother, believers should avoid causing him to stumble. Though nothing is unclean in itself, eating against conscience or grieving another through food violates love. God’s kingdom concerns righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost rather than meals. Peace and mutual strengthening take priority over exercising liberty. What is done in doubt rather than faith is sin.

chapters.title: Mutual welcome and Paul’s mission plans

parts.text: The strong should bear the weak and seek their neighbours’ good, following Christ’s selfless example. Earlier Scriptures provide patience, comfort, and hope. Paul prays for unity in glorifying God and urges mutual welcome. Christ confirmed the fathers’ promises and brought Gentiles to praise God’s mercy, as several Scriptures testify. Paul asks that hope abound through the Holy Ghost.

He explains his ministry to Gentiles and his aim to preach where Christ is not yet known. Having served from Jerusalem toward Illyricum, he hopes to visit Rome on a journey to Spain. First he must carry Macedonia’s and Achaia’s contribution to Jerusalem’s poor saints. He requests prayer for safety, acceptance of this service, and a joyful visit to Rome.

chapters.title: Greetings, a warning about division, and praise

parts.text: Paul commends Phebe and asks the Romans to receive and assist her. He greets Priscilla and Aquila, who risked their lives for him, the church in their house, and many fellow labourers, friends, relatives, and households. The greetings recognize varied service, endurance, hospitality, and affection within the Christian community.

He warns them to avoid those causing divisions contrary to the teaching they received, whose flattering speech conceals self-interest. He commends their obedience and promises that God will shortly bruise Satan under their feet. Companions, including Tertius who wrote the letter, send greetings. Paul closes by praising God’s power to establish them through the gospel and the once-hidden mystery now made known to all nations for faith’s obedience.
